title: Diabetes in Romania: Symptoms and Treatment · Global Health
description: More than 1.3 million Romanians live with diabetes, while many cases remain undiagnosed. Learn the causes, warning signs, treatments and future developments.
h2: Diabetes in Romania: Understanding the Scale of the Problem
Reference Institutions and Resources in Romania
Ready to speak with a doctor?

faqs.question: How many Romanians have diabetes?
faqs.answer: According to the PREDATORR study (SRDNBM), approximately 11.6% of Romania's adult population has diabetes mellitus and 16.5% has prediabetes. INSP recorded 1,485,087 people in medical records in 2024, including 114,904 diagnosed that year. The IDF estimates that approximately 1.3 million adults had diabetes in 2024, comparable with the European average.

faqs.question: What are the early signs of diabetes?
faqs.answer: The most common signs include excessive thirst, frequent urination (especially at night), persistent fatigue, blurred vision, slow wound healing, constant hunger even after eating, and tingling or numbness in the hands and feet. Type 2 diabetes can develop slowly and silently — many people have no symptoms for years before diagnosis. If you have risk factors, ask your family doctor about fasting blood glucose or HbA1c, even if you have no symptoms.

faqs.question: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
faqs.answer: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. It requires lifelong insulin therapy and usually begins in childhood or early adulthood. Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body becomes resistant to insulin or does not produce enough — it is strongly associated with lifestyle factors such as diet, physical inactivity and excess weight, and accounts for more than 90% of cases in Romania. The two forms have different causes, treatments and clinical courses, but both require careful management to prevent complications.

faqs.question: What are the best treatments for type 2 diabetes in Romania?
faqs.answer: First-line treatment usually includes metformin alongside lifestyle changes. Newer medicine classes — GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide/Ozempic) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin/Jardiance, dapagliflozin/Forxiga) — have transformed treatment by lowering blood glucose while protecting the heart and kidneys. The ADA 2025 guidelines recommend these classes for patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Treatment is always individualised to the patient's profile.

faqs.question: How often should I have check-ups if I have diabetes in Romania?
faqs.answer: If you have diagnosed diabetes, you should have at least one structured annual review with your family doctor or diabetes specialist — including HbA1c, blood pressure, kidney function, cholesterol, weight, foot examination and diabetic retinopathy screening. More frequent HbA1c tests, every 3–6 months, are recommended if blood glucose is not well controlled or treatment has recently changed.

faqs.question: Can diabetes go into remission?
faqs.answer: Type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission — defined as achieving near-normal blood glucose without medication — through significant weight loss, often after bariatric surgery or a very-low-calorie diet. The landmark DiRECT trial showed remission in approximately 50% of participants after one year of a structured dietary programme. This does not mean the underlying predisposition has disappeared — remission requires sustained lifestyle changes to continue. There is currently no cure for type 1 diabetes, although stem-cell therapies in clinical trials aim to restore insulin production in the coming years.

faqs.question: Can I consult a doctor online about diabetes in Romania?
faqs.answer: Yes. Global Health offers online general-practice consultations with registered doctors — including diabetes assessment, symptom evaluation, medication review and referrals for tests (including HbA1c, fasting blood glucose and a full metabolic panel). Book at myglobalhealth.online or email globalhealth@myglobalhealth.online.

body: All articlesEndocrinologieDiabetes: The Silent DiseaseDiabetes mellitus is one of the most widespread chronic diseases in Romania—and one of the most underestimated. With the correct diagnosis, appropriate treatment and regular monitoring, people with diabetes can live full, healthy lives, especially thanks to recent advances such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.Global Health Medical TeamJuly 19, 202619 min read Causes, Symptoms, Treatments and the Future of Care An estimated 1.3 million Romanians live with diabetes — and thousands more cases remain undiagnosed. This guide covers everything you need to know: causes, warning signs, the best treatments available today, the importance of regular check-ups, and emerging therapies that could transform diabetes care in the years ahead. — Evidence-based — Aligned with SRDNBM and CNAS — Updated June 2026 — Written by Dr Tiago Miguel Figueira · Ordem dos Médicos no. 77986 · Clinical Director, Global Health TF Written by Dr. Tiago Miguel Figueira Clinical Director · Ordem dos Médicos no. 77986 · General and Family Medicine 10 MIN READ Diabetes mellitus is one of the most prevalent chronic diseases in Romania — and, at the same time, one of the most underestimated. It is often called the “silent disease” because type 2 diabetes, which accounts for more than 90% of cases, can develop slowly over several years without noticeable symptoms. By the time it is diagnosed, the disease has often already been present for some time. The good news is that diabetes can be managed very effectively. With the right diagnosis, appropriate treatment and regular monitoring, people with diabetes can live full and healthy lives. With the remarkable therapeutic advances of the past decade — particularly the arrival of GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors — the clinical options available in Romania today are better than ever. Section 01 Diabetes in Romania: Understanding the Scale of the Problem According to the PREDATORR epidemiological study conducted by Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases (SRDNBM) between 2012 and 2014 — Romania's only national diabetes prevalence study — approximately 11.6% of the adult population has diabetes mellitus and 16.5% has prediabetes. According to data from the National Institute of Public Health (INSP), 1,485,087 people were recorded in medical records in 2024, including 114,904 diagnosed that year. Estimates from the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) indicate that approximately 1.3 million adults aged 20 to 79 had diabetes in Romania in 2024, a prevalence comparable with the European average. 11.6% Of the adult population has diabetes mellitus (PREDATORR study, SRDNBM) 16.5% Of the adult population has prediabetes 1.48M People recorded in medical records in 2024 (INSP) 1.3M Adults aged 20–79 estimated by the IDF to have diabetes in 2024 Sources: Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases — PREDATORR study; National Institute of Public Health (INSP); National Health Insurance House (CNAS); International Diabetes Federation — Diabetes Atlas 2024. According to data from the National Health Insurance House (CNAS), only about 1.3 million patients with diabetes receive treatment through the National Diabetes Mellitus Programme — just over half of all estimated cases. The difference represents either people who do not take medication or cases that remain undiagnosed, confirming the global trend. A distinctive feature of the Romanian system, highlighted by SRDNBM, is that diabetes care is provided exclusively by physicians specialising in diabetes, nutrition and metabolic diseases — a standalone specialty found in few countries worldwide. Could you be at risk without knowing it? A significant proportion of people with type 2 diabetes in Romania remain undiagnosed. If you have risk factors — a family history of diabetes, excess weight, high blood pressure or physical inactivity — ask your family doctor about a fasting blood glucose test or HbA1c. Early diagnosis is essential for preventing complications. Section 02 Types of Diabetes Not all diabetes is the same. Understanding the type you have — or are at risk of developing — is the first step towards effective management. 🔵 Type 1 Diabetes Autoimmune · Insulin-dependent The immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. The body produces little or no insulin. Lifelong insulin therapy is required. It usually develops in childhood or early adulthood. 🟠 Type 2 Diabetes Lifestyle & genetics · Progressive The body becomes resistant to insulin or does not produce enough. It is strongly associated with lifestyle factors. It is the most common form in Romania, accounting for more than 90% of cases. It can initially be controlled with diet, exercise and oral medication, although many patients eventually need insulin. 🟡 Gestational Diabetes Pregnancy-related · Usually temporary It develops during pregnancy when hormonal changes affect how insulin works. It usually resolves after delivery but significantly increases the lifelong risk of type 2 diabetes for both mother and child. Recent research shows an increasing incidence of this form of diabetes in Romania, with narrowing differences between urban and rural areas. ⚪ Prediabetes Preventable · Often reversible Blood glucose is higher than normal but does not meet the diagnostic thresholds for diabetes. This is a critical opportunity for intervention — lifestyle changes at this stage can prevent or significantly delay type 2 diabetes. According to SRDNBM, 16.5% of Romania's adult population is in this situation, often without knowing it. Section 03 Causes and Risk Factors Type 1 Diabetes The exact cause of type 1 diabetes remains incompletely understood. It is an autoimmune disease — the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Genetic factors play a role, as may exposure to certain viral infections. Research in this field is coordinated in Romania through institutes such as the “N.C. Paulescu” National Institute of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases in Bucharest, alongside specialist societies such as SRDNBM. Type 2 Diabetes Type 2 diabetes has a more complex and modifiable set of causes, combining genetic predisposition with lifestyle and environmental factors. The central mechanism is insulin resistance — the body's cells no longer respond effectively to insulin — together with a progressive decline in the pancreas's ability to compensate by producing more. ⚖️ Excess body weight Abdominal, or visceral, fat in particular. Obesity is the most important modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes. 🛋️ Physical inactivity Sedentary behaviour reduces insulin sensitivity. More than 80% of adults in Romania report no weekly leisure-time aerobic activity — one of the highest percentages in the EU. 🍞 Diet high in ultra-processed foods High consumption of refined carbohydrates, sugar and ultra-processed foods is strongly associated with insulin resistance. 👨‍👩‍👧 Family history Having a first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes significantly increases your personal risk of developing the disease. 🎂 Age over 45 Risk increases with age. According to INSP data, diabetes prevalence is significantly higher among older people. 🩺 High blood pressure or dyslipidaemia Metabolic risk factors tend to cluster. High blood pressure and lipid disorders often coexist with insulin resistance. 🤰 Previous gestational diabetes Women who have had gestational diabetes face a considerably higher lifetime risk of developing type 2 diabetes. 🚬 Smoking Smoking increases the risk of type 2 diabetes and worsens cardiovascular outcomes in people with diabetes. Quitting is recommended as part of comprehensive disease management. Section 04 Signs and Symptoms Symptoms vary considerably between type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Type 1 often presents acutely — with rapidly developing symptoms that may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency. Type 2, by contrast, usually develops slowly and silently over several years, with symptoms so mild or gradual that many people attribute them to ageing, stress or tiredness. 💧 Excessive thirst Persistent, difficult-to-quench thirst — polydipsia — as the kidneys work hard to filter excess glucose. 🚽 Frequent urination Polyuria, especially at night (nocturia). Often the most troublesome initial symptom. 😴 Persistent fatigue Constant exhaustion even after adequate rest, caused by cells being deprived of glucose as an energy source. ⚖️ Unexplained weight loss Especially in type 1 — the body breaks down fat and muscle for energy when insulin is absent. 👁️ Blurred vision High blood glucose causes changes in the eye's lens, temporarily affecting focus. 🩹 Slow wound healing Impaired circulation and immune function slow the healing of cuts, wounds and infections. 🤚 Tingling or numbness Peripheral neuropathy — affecting the hands and feet — can be an early sign, particularly in type 2. 🍽️ Constant hunger Polyphagia — persistent hunger even after eating — occurs when cells cannot absorb glucose effectively. When to seek emergency care: If you or a family member develops sudden intense thirst, excessive urination, vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion or acetone-smelling breath — especially in a child or young adult — this may be diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency. Call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department. Section 05 Current Diabetes Treatments in Romania Diabetes treatment has undergone a genuine revolution over the past decade. In Romania, the Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases (SRDNBM) sets the reference clinical guidelines, aligned with international American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommendations. Access to medicines and reimbursement conditions are regulated through the National Diabetes Mellitus Programme, administered by the National Health Insurance House (CNAS). Lifestyle Changes — The Foundation of Every Treatment For both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, lifestyle is the foundation of disease management. For type 2 in particular, dietary changes and increased physical activity can significantly reduce HbA1c, improve insulin sensitivity and, in some cases — especially after bariatric surgery or a very-low-calorie diet — lead to sustained remission. Structured education programmes delivered in diabetes clinics provide evidence-based support for lifestyle management. Medication The main classes of medicines available in Romania are outlined below. Treatment decisions are individualised — the SRDNBM and ADA 2025 guidelines emphasise a patient-centred approach that considers cardiovascular risk, kidney function, weight and personal preferences. First line · Type 2 Metformin Glucophage · Generics (reimbursed by CNAS) The established first-line oral medicine for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood glucose by reducing hepatic glucose production. Well tolerated, affordable and widely available, it remains the standard starting point in most type 2 treatment plans in Romania. Cardiorenal protection GLP-1 receptor agonists Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) · Liraglutide (Victoza) A transformative class of injectable, and now oral, medicines that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1. They lower blood glucose, promote significant weight loss and reduce cardiovascular risk. The ADA 2025 guidelines prioritise them for patients with established cardiovascular disease or high risk. Available by prescription in Romania. Cardiorenal protection SGLT2 inhibitors Empagliflozin (Jardiance) · Dapagliflozin (Forxiga) These tablets lower blood glucose by causing excess sugar to be excreted in urine. They independently protect the heart and kidneys — and are recommended as first-line treatment for patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease, regardless of HbA1c. There is a strong evidence base from the EMPA-REG OUTCOME and CREDENCE trials. Glycaemic control DPP-4 inhibitors Sitagliptin (Januvia) · Linagliptin (Trajenta) Oral tablets that stimulate insulin secretion according to blood glucose levels. They are weight-neutral and have a low risk of hypoglycaemia. They are often used when GLP-1 receptor agonists or SGLT2 inhibitors are not tolerated or suitable. Type 1 and advanced type 2 Insulin therapy Basal, bolus and premixed insulins · Insulin pumps Essential for all patients with type 1 and many with type 2. Modern insulin analogues provide more predictable action profiles than older formulations. Insulin pumps are available for selected patients and reimbursed through the health insurance system. Type 1 · New standard Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) FreeStyle Libre · Dexcom · Medtronic CGM removes the need for finger-prick tests, provides real-time glucose trends and alerts, and improves glycaemic control. Access to CGM is reimbursed for patients with type 1 diabetes under certain conditions set by CNAS. Closed-loop systems are available in specialist centres. ADA 2025 guideline update: The ADA 2025 guidelines emphasise that GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors should be prioritised for patients with type 2 diabetes who have established cardiovascular disease or high risk, heart failure or chronic kidney disease — regardless of HbA1c. If you have type 2 diabetes and any of these conditions, ask your doctor whether these treatment classes are suitable for you. Section 06 The Importance of Regular Check-ups Diabetes is a chronic disease that progresses over time, and its complications — if not detected — can be serious and irreversible. Diabetic retinopathy is one of the leading causes of blindness among working-age adults in Romania. Diabetic nephropathy is a major cause of end-stage chronic kidney disease. Peripheral neuropathy causes diabetic foot complications that, in severe cases, can lead to amputation. Decades of research show that all these complications can largely be prevented — or significantly delayed — through good glycaemic control, blood pressure management and regular monitoring. A structured annual diabetes review is one of the best-supported and most effective interventions in medicine. What Your Annual Diabetes Review Should Include HbA1c measurement (average blood glucose over the past 3 months) Blood pressure measurement and review of antihypertensive treatment Kidney function — estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio Cholesterol and a full lipid profile Weight and body mass index (BMI) assessment Foot examination — including pulse and sensation assessment Diabetic retinopathy screening — fundus examination or retinal photography Medication review and adjustment if needed Assessment of adherence to the diabetes self-management plan Smoking status assessment and cessation support where appropriate Influenza vaccination (strongly recommended for people with diabetes) Screening for People Without a Diagnosis If you have risk factors for type 2 diabetes and have never been tested, your family doctor can request fasting blood glucose or HbA1c — simple tests available in laboratories throughout the country. This is especially important if you are over 45, have a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure or were overweight during pregnancy. Early detection of prediabetes provides a genuine opportunity to prevent or delay type 2 diabetes through lifestyle changes. Diabetic retinopathy screening in Romania: The Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases recommends annual diabetic retinopathy screening by fundus examination or retinal photography for every patient with diabetes. If you have diabetes and have not had this check recently, speak to your diabetes specialist or family doctor. Section 07 The Future of Diabetes Treatment The pace of innovation in diabetes medicine is unprecedented. Several research areas — some already in advanced clinical trials — have the potential to fundamentally change what it means to live with diabetes over the next decade. Phase 1/2/3 · Regulatory submission in 2026 Stem Cell Therapy (beta cells) Zimislecel (formerly VX-880), developed by Vertex Pharmaceuticals, involves infusing fully differentiated insulin-producing islet cells derived from stem cells into the hepatic portal vein — with the aim of restoring endogenous insulin production in type 1 diabetes. By June 2025, the pivotal trial included 50 participants, with regulatory submission expected in 2026. A review published in PMC (2025) describes this approach as potentially “transformative”. Clinical development Artificial Pancreas Automated closed-loop insulin delivery systems — combining continuous glucose monitoring with automated insulin pumps — already represent a major advance for patients with type 1. The next generation incorporates machine-learning algorithms to anticipate glucose fluctuations before they occur. Emerging therapies Dual and Triple Receptor Agonists Tirzepatide (Mounjaro), a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist, has achieved greater HbA1c reductions and weight loss than existing GLP-1 agonists and is already available in Romania. Triple agonists (GLP-1/GIP/glucagon) are in advanced clinical trials and may offer even greater metabolic benefits. Immunotherapy research Immune Modulation in Type 1 Teplizumab, an anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody, has been shown in clinical trials to delay the clinical onset of type 1 diabetes by approximately two years in people at high risk. Research into immune checkpoint inhibitors and tolerance induction continues, with the aim of preserving residual beta-cell function at diagnosis. Precision medicine Genomics and AI-Guided Treatment Genomic profiling is beginning to identify diabetes subtypes that respond differently to specific medicines. Artificial intelligence-based continuous glucose monitoring systems that learn individual metabolic patterns and provide personalised recommendations are in development. Regenerative medicine Beta-Cell Encapsulation A parallel strategy to stem-cell transplantation involves encapsulating insulin-producing cells in protective biomaterial devices that shield them from immune destruction — potentially removing the need for immunosuppression. The University of Miami Diabetes Research Institute has demonstrated proof of concept in clinical trials, with the first patient achieving insulin independence. Stem-cell therapy for type 1 diabetes is examined in detail in a 2025 publication in PMC (PMID: PMC12689004), which concludes that “stem cell therapy offers a dual strategy: regeneration of insulin-producing beta cells and regulation of immune responses”. Although a definitive cure remains a future goal, the direction of research is more promising than ever. Section 08 Reference Institutions and Resources in Romania If you live with diabetes in Romania, or are concerned about your risk of developing it, the following organisations and services are your main reference points for clinical care, education and support. 🩺 Romanian Society of Diabetes (SRDNBM) 🏥 CNAS — National Diabetes Programme 📊 National Institute of Public Health 📋 Ministry of Health 🔬 “N.C. Paulescu” Institute 📋 Romanian College of Physicians 🚑 Emergency services — 112 Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases (SRDNBM) SRDNBM is Romania's leading scientific authority on all aspects of diabetes care. It is responsible for the PREDATORR epidemiological study — the largest diabetes prevalence study conducted in Romania — and issues annual statements and awareness materials for World Diabetes Day on 14 November. CNAS and the National Diabetes Mellitus Programme The National Health Insurance House administers the National Diabetes Mellitus Programme, which reimburses medicines and medical devices for people with a diagnosis. CNAS data, correlated with National Institute of Statistics data, are used to monitor the disease nationally. National Institute of Public Health (INSP) INSP, through the National Centre for Public Health Statistics and Informatics, publishes detailed annual epidemiological data on diabetes prevalence and incidence by county, essential for public-health policy planning. “N.C. Paulescu” National Institute of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases The “N.C. Paulescu” Institute in Bucharest is Romania's main referral centre for diabetes and metabolic disease diagnosis, treatment and research, and also provides therapeutic education programmes for patients. Section 09 Frequently Asked Questions How many Romanians have diabetes? According to the PREDATORR study (SRDNBM), approximately 11.6% of Romania's adult population has diabetes mellitus and 16.5% has prediabetes. INSP recorded 1,485,087 people in medical records in 2024, including 114,904 diagnosed that year. The IDF estimates that approximately 1.3 million adults had diabetes in 2024, comparable with the European average. What are the early signs of diabetes? The most common signs include excessive thirst, frequent urination (especially at night), persistent fatigue, blurred vision, slow wound healing, constant hunger even after eating, and tingling or numbness in the hands and feet. Type 2 diabetes can develop slowly and silently — many people have no symptoms for years before diagnosis. If you have risk factors, ask your family doctor about fasting blood glucose or HbA1c, even if you have no symptoms. What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes? Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. It requires lifelong insulin therapy and usually begins in childhood or early adulthood. Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body becomes resistant to insulin or does not produce enough — it is strongly associated with lifestyle factors such as diet, physical inactivity and excess weight, and accounts for more than 90% of cases in Romania. The two forms have different causes, treatments and clinical courses, but both require careful management to prevent complications. What are the best treatments for type 2 diabetes in Romania? First-line treatment usually includes metformin alongside lifestyle changes. Newer medicine classes — GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide/Ozempic) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin/Jardiance, dapagliflozin/Forxiga) — have transformed treatment by lowering blood glucose while protecting the heart and kidneys. The ADA 2025 guidelines recommend these classes for patients with established cardiovascular disease, heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Treatment is always individualised to the patient's profile. How often should I have check-ups if I have diabetes in Romania? If you have diagnosed diabetes, you should have at least one structured annual review with your family doctor or diabetes specialist — including HbA1c, blood pressure, kidney function, cholesterol, weight, foot examination and diabetic retinopathy screening. More frequent HbA1c tests, every 3–6 months, are recommended if blood glucose is not well controlled or treatment has recently changed. Can diabetes go into remission? Type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission — defined as achieving near-normal blood glucose without medication — through significant weight loss, often after bariatric surgery or a very-low-calorie diet. The landmark DiRECT trial showed remission in approximately 50% of participants after one year of a structured dietary programme. This does not mean the underlying predisposition has disappeared — remission requires sustained lifestyle changes to continue. There is currently no cure for type 1 diabetes, although stem-cell therapies in clinical trials aim to restore insulin production in the coming years. Can I consult a doctor online about diabetes in Romania? Yes. Global Health offers online general-practice consultations with registered doctors — including diabetes assessment, symptom evaluation, medication review and referrals for tests (including HbA1c, fasting blood glucose and a full metabolic panel). Book at myglobalhealth.online or email globalhealth@myglobalhealth.online. Medical Notice Written by Dr Tiago Miguel Figueira (Ordem dos Médicos no. 77986), Clinical Director at Global Health. This article is for general information and education only and does not constitute personalised medical advice. The information is based on data from the Romanian Society of Diabetes, Nutrition and Metabolic Diseases, CNAS and INSP, the ADA 2025 guidelines, and peer-reviewed scientific literature, updated to June 2026. If you have symptoms of diabetes or a medical emergency, call 112 or go to the nearest emergency department. Questions about diabetes? Speak to a doctor today. Online general-practice consultations with registered doctors. Available in Romanian, English, Portuguese, Arabic and other languages. title: Lower blood pressure quickly: safe first steps
description: What to do after a high reading, when to call 112 and why extra captopril, additional doses and improvised remedies may be unsafe.
h1: How to lower blood pressure quickly: safe steps and when to call 112
h2: How can you lower blood pressure quickly and safely?
What you can do straight away without putting yourself at risk
When high blood pressure may accompany an emergency
There is no universal reading for taking captopril or an extra dose
Repeated high readings are usually managed through family medicine
What to have ready for a scheduled consultation

faqs.question: What lowers blood pressure immediately at home?
faqs.answer: No remedy is safe for every situation. Check symptoms and, if stable, take two careful readings. Call 112 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or neurological signs.

faqs.question: At what blood pressure should I take captopril?
faqs.answer: There is no universal number. Take it only if prescribed and according to your personal plan. Never take an extra dose or unprescribed medicine.

faqs.question: Will lemon, garlic or tea lower blood pressure quickly?
faqs.answer: They do not treat an emergency. Rest may coincide with a lower reading but does not cancel serious symptoms; some herbal products interact with medicines.

faqs.question: When is a scheduled consultation enough?
faqs.answer: When stable, without warning signs, and repeated high readings need assessment. If a reading remains around 180/110 mmHg or higher, seek same-day assessment through family medicine, an out-of-hours centre or an emergency department; add cardiology for a clinical reason.

Do not start with an improvised tablet.No food, tea or tablet lowers blood pressure quickly and safely for everyone. Call 112 if a high reading occurs with chest pain, severe breathlessness, one-sided weakness or numbness, speech difficulty, confusion, fainting, sudden vision loss or a sudden, unusually severe headache. Do not wait or drive. Without these signs, stop exertion, sit quietly and take two careful readings a short time apart. Do not take extra captopril, someone else’s medicine or a leftover dose without personal instructions.Acute chest, breathing or neurological signs: call 112Repeat the measurement correctly if you are stableDo not improvise medicines or dosesChronic-care consultationOpen the blood pressure logThe right orderWarning symptoms take priority over another measurement.Pain, exertion, anxiety or technique can alter a reading.A forced rapid fall can be dangerous; treatment is individual.GHGlobal Health Medical TeamAfter a high readingWhat you can do straight away without putting yourself at riskStop exerting yourself, sit down and check for symptoms before you repeat the measurement.Support your back, keep both feet on the floor and rest your arm at heart level.Use a correctly sized cuff on your bare upper arm and do not talk while the monitor is running.After a few minutes of rest, take two readings a short time apart and write them down.Record your pulse, symptoms, the time, usual medicines and relevant context such as pain, fever or exertion.These steps do not treat hypertension. They reduce errors and give a clinician useful information. Do not keep measuring until you see the number you want or record only the lowest result.If the reading stays around 180/110 mmHg or higher, seek assessment that day to exclude a hypertensive emergency through family medicine, an out-of-hours centre or an emergency department. If you become worse or a warning sign appears, call 112.Warning signsWhen high blood pressure may accompany an emergencyA hypertensive emergency combines very high blood pressure with acute organ injury. At home, you can recognise warning signs but not confirm the diagnosis.Chest pain or pressure, especially with sweating, nausea or a feeling that you may faint.Severe breathlessness or rapidly worsening breathing.A drooping face, weakness or numbness on one side, or slurred speech.New confusion, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness.Sudden loss of vision or an explosive headache unlike your usual headaches.Call 112, do not drive and note when symptoms began. Have your medication list ready and follow the dispatcher. A lower second reading does not cancel a possible stroke or heart-attack symptom.Pregnancy and after birthA high reading with severe headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, vomiting, breathlessness or sudden swelling needs urgent obstetric assessment. title: Low blood pressure: causes, what to do, and when to call 112
description: What low blood pressure means, the common causes, the steps recommended by the European guideline when you feel dizzy, why sugar water doesn't help, and when it's an emergency.
h1: Low blood pressure: why it happens, what to do right away, and when not to wait
h2: Low blood pressure: causes, what to do right away, and when to see a doctor
What low blood pressure means, and when it matters
Common causes of low blood pressure
What to do when you have low blood pressure and feel dizzy
What actually raises low blood pressure, and what only seems to
When to see a doctor for low blood pressure
Ready to speak with a doctor?

faqs.question: Is a blood pressure of 90 over 60 dangerous?
faqs.answer: With no symptoms, usually not, and it isn't treated. With dizziness, fainting, or if it appeared alongside a new medication, it's worth a consultation.

faqs.question: What should I drink when my blood pressure is low?
faqs.answer: Water, drunk quickly. Sugar adds nothing extra. For coffee, the evidence is very weak.

faqs.question: What raises low blood pressure quickly?
faqs.answer: Sitting or lying down with your legs raised, crossing your legs and tensing your muscles, and water. These are the steps from the European guideline. Medications that raise blood pressure are prescription-only.

faqs.question: When is low blood pressure an emergency?
faqs.answer: When it comes with fainting and chest pain, laboured breathing, confusion, bleeding, high fever, or cold, clammy skin. Call 112.

The common causes, the steps that actually raise blood pressure within minutes, what doesn't help, and the short checklist for calling 112.Global Health Medical TeamSeptember 7, 20268 min readClinically reviewed by Dr Tiago Miguel FigueiraGlobal Health · Healthcare anytime, anywhere General medicineRomânia · Hypotension guideLow blood pressure: causes, what to do right away, and when to see a doctorA blood pressure of 90 over 60 in someone who feels fine isn't something to treat. The same reading with dizziness, blurred vision, or fainting has causes that can be found.Low blood pressure, meaning under 90/60 mmHg, isn't a disease in itself. If you have no symptoms, the guidelines are clear that it doesn't need treatment. The problem appears when blood pressure drops by 20 mmHg or more on standing up and brings on dizziness, blacked-out vision, or fainting. In that case, the right response on the spot is to sit or lie down with your legs raised, drink water, and cross your legs while tensing your muscles. Sugar water, vitamins, and teas don't appear in any guideline. Fainting with chest pain, laboured breathing, or confusion means calling 112.Under 90/60 mmHg with no symptoms: usually doesn't need treatmentA drop of 20/10 mmHg on standing, within 3 minutes: orthostatic hypotensionOn the spot: sit or lie down, legs raised, water, tensed musclesESC guideline for syncopeNormal blood pressure by ageThe right orderMeasure correctly for seven days before calling yourself hypotensive.Look for the cause before the remedy: dehydration, heat, a new medication, a large meal.Repeated fainting needs investigating, not treating with coffee.GHGlobal Health Medical TeamReviewed by the Global Health medical team.DefinitionsWhat low blood pressure means, and when it mattersThe same term covers two different situations, and only one of them needs treatment.The first is constantly low blood pressure, under 90/60 mmHg, in someone who feels fine. The NHS and NHLBI say the same thing: with no symptoms, it usually isn't treated. The second is orthostatic hypotension: the European guideline defines it as a drop in systolic pressure of at least 20 mmHg, or in diastolic pressure of 10 mmHg, within the first 3 minutes after standing up. This is what causes the dizziness on getting out of bed and the blackout in front of your eyes, and this is the one worth investigating.ESC 2018 guideline for syncope, NHS — low blood pressure, NHLBI. Accessed 7 September 2026.Where it comes fromCommon causes of low blood pressureMost causes are minor and reversible. A few aren't, which is why the list is worth going through.Low fluid intake: dehydration, heat, diarrhoea, vomiting. The most common cause in summer.Medications: diuretics, vasodilators, some antidepressants, heart and blood pressure medications, some sedatives. Check what you've started recently.After a meal: postprandial hypotension, especially in older adults and after large meals.Standing for long periods, prolonged bed rest, alcohol.Pregnancy, especially in the first two trimesters.Heart: heart failure, arrhythmias, heart attack.Nervous system: diabetes with nerve damage, Parkinson's disease.Addison's disease (adrenal insufficiency), where blood pressure drops mainly on changing position.Bleeding or severe infection: low blood pressure with a fast pulse, cold, clammy skin. An emergency.ESC 2018, causes table and MedlinePlus — hypotension.The European guidelineWhat to do when you have low blood pressure and feel dizzyThe steps below come from the ESC guideline and NHS recommendations. They work within minutes and cost nothing.Sit or lie down immediately, with your legs raised above heart level. If you can't, sit with your head between your knees.Counter-pressure manoeuvres: cross your legs and tense your thighs and buttocks, clench your fists, rise onto your toes. The guideline rates these class IIa, meaning recommended.Drink water. The guideline mentions rapid water intake; adequate hydration carries the same class of recommendation.Get up slowly, in stages: sit on the edge of the bed, then stand, with support.Long term, for confirmed orthostatic hypotension, the guideline recommends 2–3 litres of fluids a day, extra salt only on a doctor's advice, compression stockings, sleeping with the head of the bed raised, and cutting back on medications that lower blood pressure. Midodrine and fludrocortisone exist, but they're a specialist's decision, by prescription.ESC 2018, section 5.3 and NHS — fainting.Sugar water, vitamins, teasWhat actually raises low blood pressure, and what only seems toThe remedies most people look for don't appear in any European guideline. They aren't dangerous, but they don't do what people think either.Sugar water: the guidelines recommend water; sugar doesn't appear anywhere. Plain water does the same job.Coffee: a 2021 systematic review found only very small studies with inconsistent results, and recommends caffeine only after evidence-based treatments have been exhausted. It isn't a treatment.Vitamins: no vitamin appears in the guidelines as a treatment for low blood pressure. If the hypotension comes from anaemia or an endocrine condition, the underlying cause is treated, after testing.Teas, chocolate, extra salt: no evidence. The ESC guideline allows for increased salt intake only as a doctor-directed measure, in selected patients.When to call 112Fainting with chest pain, laboured breathing, a fast or irregular heartbeat, confusion, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech. Fainting during exercise or while lying down. Black stools, vomiting blood, high fever with low blood pressure, cold and clammy skin. The person doesn't fully recover within a minute. Calling 112 is free, from any network.Clinical Autonomic Research 2021, caffeine in orthostatic hypotension; Gov.ro — the 112 emergency service.Not an emergency, but worth an appointmentWhen to see a doctor for low blood pressureWhen the dizziness keeps recurring, when you've fainted once with no explanation, or when the low blood pressure appeared alongside a new medication.A family doctor or general practitioner can do the three things that matter: measuring blood pressure lying down and standing up, reviewing your medication list, and a basic set of tests, full blood count, blood glucose, thyroid function, electrolytes, plus an electrocardiogram. In an online doctor consultation with Global Health, you can go through your history and medication list and get referrals for tests. The standing measurement and the ECG still need to be done in person.Beforehand, measure for seven days, morning and evening, two readings a minute apart, seated, after five minutes of rest, with a validated upper-arm blood pressure monitor. A single low reading on a hot day doesn't mean anything; a low average, together with symptoms, does.Measurement protocol from the ESC 2024 guideline.Global Health RomâniaThe next stepYou can carry out the on-the-spot steps yourself. title: Medical letter in Romania: who issues it · Global Health
description: The medical letter in Romania: who issues it, what it must contain, what it is used for, how long it is valid and what to do if it is incomplete.
h1: The medical letter in Romania: who issues it, what it contains and what it is for
h2: What the medical letter actually is
What it must contain to be accepted
How long a medical letter stays valid
What a private online consultation can and cannot do
What to do when the letter is not good enough
Ready to speak with a doctor?

faqs.question: What is the scrisoare medicală?
faqs.answer: It is the document through which a specialist or hospital tells your family doctor the diagnosis, the investigations performed and the treatment recommendations. Within the insurance system it has a single standard form published by CNAS and is drawn up in two copies, one of which stays with the issuing doctor.

faqs.question: Who issues the medical letter?
faqs.answer: The doctor who assessed you: the outpatient specialist, the hospital on discharge, or your family doctor, depending on the purpose. A private doctor may issue a medical letter for private use, but documents reimbursed from the insurance fund belong to doctors contracted to the health insurance house.

faqs.question: How long is a medical letter valid?
faqs.answer: It depends on the purpose. For continuing chronic treatment the reference is the therapeutic protocol for the condition and the norms in force; for a file, the deadline is set by the institution requesting it. Both change, so confirm with CNAS and with the requesting institution.

faqs.question: What must it contain to be accepted?
faqs.answer: The patient's details, the date of issue, the issuing unit and doctor with stamp and signature, the full diagnosis, the investigations with their results, the recommended treatment with dose and duration, and the review date. Check the document before leaving the consulting room — a field is far easier to complete on the spot than a week later.

faqs.question: I need a medical letter for the disability commission. Is it the same document?
faqs.answer: It is the same type of document, but the commission uses its own model with specific fields. Ask the institution for the exact model, in writing, and take it to the appointment; otherwise the document risks being refused on form rather than on content.

faqs.question: Can I obtain a medical letter online?
faqs.answer: A private online consultation can issue a medical letter or report for private use, interpret the results you already have and put your file in order. The referral note and the subsidised prescription, however, remain within the health insurance pathway.

Who may issue it, what it must contain, how long it stays valid and what to do when the one you were handed is incomplete.Global Health Medical TeamAugust 14, 202610 min readClinically reviewed by Dr Andreea Lorena BicaRomania · Patient guideIt is written by one doctor for another, but the person who pays for anything missing from it is you.The scrisoare medicală — the medical letter — is the document through which a specialist or a hospital tells your family doctor the diagnosis, the investigations done and the treatment recommendations. Within the social health insurance system it has a single standard form published by CNAS, and that form opens with «Stimate(ă) coleg(ă)» precisely because it is a communication between doctors. On the strength of it, your family doctor can carry on prescribing chronic treatment. No periods appear here: every question of that kind points at CNAS.GHGlobal Health Medical TeamReviewed by the Global Health Medical Team.Starting pointWhat the medical letter actually isIt is not a certificate and it is not an attestation. It is a letter from one doctor to another, with you as its subject.Its purpose is continuity of care. Your family doctor follows you over time but is not present at the specialist appointment and has no automatic access to what was discussed there. The medical letter carries that information back: what was found, what was ruled out, what treatment was decided and what comes next.Within the social health insurance system the form is standardised, with a single approved model, and the annexed model states that the document is drawn up in two copies, one of which stays with the issuing doctor. That is a useful detail: if you lose your copy, the practice or hospital that issued it should, in principle, still have a record of it.It is a medical document, not an administrative one — the doctor decides the content, not the patient.It travels between doctors, but it is handed to you.It underpins the continuation of treatment by your family doctor.A similar document with different content is required by the assessment commission for adults with disabilities.Standard model published by CNAS.The pathwayWho issues the medical letterThe short answer: the doctor who assessed you. The useful answer depends on why you need it.The outpatient specialist — after the specialist consultation, for your family doctor.The hospital, on discharge — together with the discharge note, so treatment can continue.Your family doctor — when the document is required by a commission, a school or an employer, in the form suited to that purpose.A doctor in the private system — may issue a medical letter or a medical report for private use; documents reimbursed from the insurance fund are, however, reserved for doctors in a contractual relationship with the health insurance house.That last distinction explains most wasted journeys. A private doctor can assess you, write up the findings and recommendations and direct you onwards, but the bilet de trimitere (referral note) and the subsidised prescription belong to the insurance pathway. Ask for it in writing before you book and take it with you to the appointment. It is the simplest way to avoid a second trip.ContentWhat it must contain to be acceptedMost rejected letters are not wrong. They are incomplete.Whatever the model, a useful medical letter carries the patient's identifying details, the date of issue, the issuing unit and doctor with stamp and signature, the reason for the assessment, the relevant history, the diagnosis, the investigations performed with their results, and the recommendations — treatment, doses, duration and the date of the next review.The full diagnosis, not merely an abbreviation or a code.The investigations the diagnosis rests on, with dates and results.The recommended treatment, with name, dose and duration — without these your family doctor has nothing on which to continue prescribing.The review date or the reassessment interval.The stamp, signature and seal of the issuing unit.For commission files, exactly the fields of the annex requested, filled in completely.Check the document before you leave the consulting room. For continuing chronic treatment it follows the therapeutic protocol for the condition and the norms in force. For a commission file or an institution, the deadline is set by whoever is asking for the document. Because both change, you will not find a number of days or months in this article: you confirm it with CNAS, or with the institution requesting it.Validity runs from the date of issue — check that the date has been filled in.For chronic treatment the reference is the therapeutic protocol, not a general rule.For files, the reference is the institution's requirement, which may be stricter.If your condition has changed in the meantime, the old document no longer describes reality, whatever the deadline says.Norms in force and therapeutic protocols: CNAS · Ministry of Health.TransparencyWhat a private online consultation can and cannot doWe say this at the outset, because it is the first question and because an honest answer saves time.A private online consultation does not issue documents reimbursed from the insurance fund — no referral note, no subsidised prescription. Those belong to doctors in a contractual relationship with the health insurance house. Any private service promising otherwise is promising something it cannot deliver.What an online consultation does handle well is the part that most often gets stuck:Clinical assessment without a waiting list, and a written document describing what was found.Interpreting results you already have and clarifying what they mean.Putting the file in order: which documents you are missing, in what order to obtain them and from whom.Recommending the right investigations, so you do not pay for tests that change nothing.A second opinion before an important decision.Monitoring between specialist reviews.You can check any doctor's registration with the Romanian College of Physicians — ours as readily as anyone else's.PracticalWhat to do when the letter is not good enoughThree situations cover almost every case in which the document is refused.A field is missing — go back to the issuing doctor to have it completed. Another doctor cannot fill in someone else's document.It is on the wrong model — ask the institution for the exact model, in writing, and take it to the appointment.It has expired for that purpose — what is needed is a reassessment, not simply a new date. A doctor who re-dates a document without seeing you is not doing you a favour.And one situation that has nothing to do with paperwork: if your condition has worsened since the last assessment, the priority is the consultation, not the document. title: Medical Review Policy — Global Health Romania
description: How Global Health writes, reviews and updates the health articles published for Romania: who writes them, which registered physician signs them off, and the editorial standards we hold ourselves to.
h1: How we write and review medical content
h2: Who reviews it, and what they check
Editorial standards we hold ourselves to
body: ReviewGlobal Health · Editorial & clinical governanceHow we write and review medical content Every clinical article we publish for Romania is drafted from primary sources, checked against them, and signed off by a named physician registered with Colegiul Medicilor din România before it reaches you — and reviewed again when the underlying rules change.Read our articlesReport an issueNamed reviewersClinical sign-off by a named, registered doctorSourced to the regulatorRules link to the body that sets themKept currentRe-reviewed at least once a year01Who writes our contentArticles begin as a draft built from verified primary sources — government guidance, national health authority publications, and the social security or insurance body documentation that applies in the country the article is written for. Drafting may involve editorial tools, but no article is published on the strength of a tool alone.Articles carry one editorial byline — the Global Health Medical Team — because drafting, sourcing and editing are a team effort rather than one person's work. Clinical accountability is not anonymous, though: a physician registered with Colegiul Medicilor din România signs the article off, and it is their name and registration number that appear on it.02Who reviews it, and what they checkBefore publication, the article is reviewed in full by a registered physician. This is not a formality: the reviewer is expected to check claims against the source material rather than simply approve the draft. That physician is named on the article, with the registration number that lets you check them yourself.AuthorThe Global Health Medical TeamEvery article is drafted, sourced and edited by our clinical editorial team, so it carries one consistent byline rather than rotating individual names.ReviewerNamed clinical sign-offA registered physician checks the article before publication, and again whenever it is materially updated. Their name and registration are published on the article.The article names the physician who signed it off, with a registration you can check yourself. A published byline reads like this:Global Health Medical Team—Clinically reviewed byDr Alexandra PalagaColegiul Medicilor din România | 159625, PediatricianThe reviewer name and registration number on our articles belong to a doctor on the public register for this market — never a placeholder.Verify on the register · Colegiul Medicilor din România03Editorial standards we hold ourselves to01Figures and thresholds are never hard-coded. Amounts, waiting periods and eligibility rules set by government or insurance bodies change over time. Where an article would otherwise state one, it links to the issuing body's own page instead, so you always see the current figure.02Every regulatory claim links to its source. Statements about entitlements, certification rules or legal processes link directly to the government department, health authority or regulator that defines them — not to a summary of a summary.03Country-specific rules are written for that country. An article about sick leave in Romania is written and reviewed for Romania, separately from the same topic in another market, because the rules genuinely differ.04Nothing here replaces an individual assessment. Articles explain how a process generally works. They do not diagnose, and they do not guarantee a specific outcome in your case — that requires an actual consultation.05Emergency guidance is never generic. Where an article mentions warning signs that warrant urgent care, it gives the emergency number that applies in this market — 112.04Keeping articles currentRegulatory content is reviewed at least once a year, or sooner if we become aware that a rule, form or process it describes has changed. Where an article has been clinically reviewed, the date of that review is shown on the article, so you can judge how current it is at a glance.If a review results in a material change to the guidance, the reviewing physician's name and the review date are updated with it.05Found something that looks wrong?Tell us. Every report is checked by a member of our clinical team, and corrections are made publicly and promptly.Report an issueThis policy describes the editorial process for the general health information published on this site. It does not apply to personalised medical advice given during a consultation, which follows separate clinical governance standards. Read our medical disclaimer.Policy last updated: September 2026

title: Normal blood pressure by age · Global Health
description: Learn which blood pressure readings are normal in adults, what changes with age, and when repeated high readings need medical review.
h1: Normal blood pressure: a practical guide by age, without misleading tables
h2: What blood pressure is considered normal in adults
What changes with age and what does not
What systolic and diastolic pressure mean
How to measure your blood pressure correctly at home
When an appointment is enough and when to seek urgent care
What an online chronic disease consultation can address
Ready to speak with a doctor?

faqs.question: Is normal blood pressure different for men and women?
faqs.answer: Not in the practical sense most adults mean. Non-pregnant adults should not use a different table based only on sex. Overall risk and clinical context change, not the definition of a clearly good or clearly high reading.

faqs.question: At what reading is blood pressure considered hypertension?
faqs.answer: A repeated clinic reading of 140/90 mmHg or above is already in the hypertension range and requires confirmation. High home readings repeated over several days also deserve discussion, even though one number alone does not establish a diagnosis.

faqs.question: Is a reading of 13 over 8 acceptable?
faqs.answer: It is not a catastrophic reading, but it is not ideal either. It is above a clearly normal reading and should be repeated correctly over several days to determine whether it is a trend or an exception.

faqs.question: Does age make higher blood pressure normal?
faqs.answer: No. Age may change how carefully treatment is managed and which target is chosen for a frail person, but it does not turn persistently high blood pressure into a normal reading.

faqs.question: When should I seek urgent medical help for my blood pressure?
faqs.answer: When a high reading occurs with warning symptoms: chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side, fainting, confusion or a sudden, severe headache. Urgency is determined by the combination of the reading and symptoms.

faqs.question: Can an online consultation genuinely help me?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly for interpreting repeated readings, reviewing treatment and deciding whether tests or cardiology input are needed. It does not replace emergency care or investigations that must be performed in person.

It does not change the fact that a reading that is too high remains too high.For the average adult, a clearly normal blood pressure is below 120/70 mmHg. If readings repeatedly rise into the 120-139 systolic or 70-89 diastolic range, they are no longer ideal and should be monitored methodically. Hypertension is confirmed through repeated measurements, ideally including readings taken outside the clinic. In practice, a confirmed clinic reading of 140/90 mmHg or higher is already in the hypertension range. This is the key point when searching for values ‘by age’: no reading suddenly becomes normal simply because you are 65 or 75.Below 120/70 is a clearly normal readingRepeated clinic readings of 140/90 require confirmation and assessmentAge changes the context, not the principles of blood pressureChronic disease consultationBlood pressure calculatorWhat this guide explainsWhich numbers genuinely guide you in adulthood and why many tables circulate without context.What changes with age and what does not, even when the internet promises a broader ‘normal’ range.How to measure at home without being alarmed by one isolated reading or falsely reassured.When an appointment is enough and when warning signs require urgent assessment.GHGlobal Health Medical TeamReviewed by the Global Health Medical Team.The short answerWhat blood pressure is considered normal in adultsThe direct answer is that below 120/70 mmHg is clearly normal, while repeated clinic readings of 140/90 mmHg are already in the hypertension range.The intermediate range causes the most confusion. Someone with a reading of 132/84 may hear ‘it is not that bad’ and assume it no longer matters. It does matter. It may not yet be confirmed hypertension, but it is not an ideal reading either and should be monitored if it recurs.Below 120/70: a clearly normal reading.Systolic 120-139 or diastolic 70-89: no longer the ideal range; repeat the measurement correctly and monitor the trend.Repeated readings of 140/90 or above: consistent with hypertension and requiring confirmation.A single reading does not establish a diagnosis on its own if it was measured incorrectly or under unfavourable circumstances.Patient information and materials from the Romanian Society of Cardiology: Cardioportal. The current European guideline remains the main clinical reference: ESC 2024.Where the misconception arisesWhat changes with age and what does notPeople search online for a separate table for ages 30, 50 or 70. Medicine looks for something else: how consistent the readings are, your overall risk and which other conditions are present.At 28, repeatedly high blood pressure matters because it has decades in which to cause harm. At 68, the same reading matters because it may occur alongside kidney disease, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, stroke or heart failure. It does not become ‘normal’ in either case.Young adult: hypertension may go unnoticed precisely because it rarely causes pain.Middle age: weight, smoking, cholesterol and blood glucose affect how closely it should be monitored.Older person: the treatment target may be individualised to avoid dizziness or falls, but this does not make a high reading acceptable.Pregnancy: this is a separate clinical situation and should not be combined with general adult tables.‘It is normal for your age’ is often a misleading statementWhat may differ for an older person is how treatment and monitoring are managed, not the definition of a reading that is too high.Two numbersWhat systolic and diastolic pressure meanSystolic pressure is the maximum pressure when the heart pumps blood. Diastolic pressure is the minimum pressure between heartbeats.The practical rule is simple: if either number is abnormal, the reading deserves attention. A reading of 152/78 is not reassuring simply because ‘the second number is good’. A reading of 126/94 is not good simply because the first number has not reached 14.High systolic pressure with a better diastolic reading: particularly common at older ages and should not be dismissed.High diastolic pressure: this also matters, especially when it recurs.Symptoms, pulse and test results help with interpretation, but they do not cancel out a series of high readings.The trend is more useful than a single number recorded on a bad morning.If you want to follow the trend rather than one isolated number, use the blood pressure calculator and record instead of treating every measurement as a final verdict.TechniqueHow to measure your blood pressure correctly at homeMany ‘bad readings’ are not truly bad; they were measured incorrectly. Correcting the technique is quicker than changing a treatment plan unnecessarily.Sit quietly for five minutes first, with your back supported and your legs uncrossed.Do not measure immediately after coffee, smoking, exercise or climbing stairs.Use an upper-arm monitor with the correct cuff size; wrist monitors are more prone to error.Keep your arm at heart level and do not talk during the measurement.Take two readings and record the time, circumstances and any symptoms.Repeat this over several days, not only after a stressful day or, conversely, an unusually calm one.A record like this makes the consultation useful. The doctor sees a pattern rather than a snapshot. Sound decisions can then be based on that pattern: simple monitoring, blood tests, an ECG, lifestyle changes or an adjustment to treatment.Cardioportal also provides patient guidance on correct home measurement: Cardioportal.The practical decisionWhen an appointment is enough and when to seek urgent careMost high readings are not an emergency. It becomes an emergency when a high reading occurs with symptoms suggesting acute harm.Book an appointment if you have high readings over several days, even if you feel well.Do not delay if you also have diabetes, kidney disease, are pregnant, have heart disease or have previously had a stroke.Seek urgent help if you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side, fainting, confusion or a sudden, severe headache.Do not take leftover ‘emergency’ medication from a previous episode without a plan agreed with your doctor.The number alone does not tell the whole storyA person with a reading of 180/110 and no symptoms does not have the same priority as someone with 170/100 plus chest pain. Symptoms change everything.What a consultation can doWhat an online chronic disease consultation can addressIt offers more than a ‘prescription renewal’: it can turn a disorganised collection of readings into a clear follow-up plan.For stable hypertension, a GP can coordinate monitoring, current treatment and the management of risk factors. During an online chronic disease consultation, your home readings, symptoms, prescribed medication, test results and cardiovascular risk can all be reviewed.If readings remain uncontrolled, symptoms develop, organ damage is suspected or specialist tests are needed, the GP may recommend cardiology or an in-person assessment. Having an organised record already available makes this transition clearer and faster.Interpretation of a properly completed home blood pressure record.Review of previously prescribed antihypertensive treatment and how well it is tolerated.Assessment of blood pressure alongside other chronic conditions: diabetes, kidney disease and dyslipidaemia.Clear guidance on when cardiology or urgent assessment is needed.That is the difference between an article that merely attracts traffic and one that can support a genuine clinical next step.Global Health RomaniaNext stepsIf you already have several readings outside the normal range, another search is not the useful next step. Review the full pattern and decide whether it requires monitoring, further tests or a change to treatment.Online chronic disease managementBlood pressure calculator and recordOur doctors in RomaniaContact Global Health RomaniaDo you have repeatedly high or fluctuating readings?Bring your recorded measurements to the consultation. title: Contact Global Health Romania | Online Doctor
description: Contact Global Health Romania: info@myglobalhealth.online. Online video consultations with registered doctors, in Romanian and English.

faqs.question: Do you have a clinic in Romania?
faqs.answer: No. We operate online only in Romania. Our registered office is in Ireland and consultations happen by video call.

faqs.question: Are your doctors registered in Romania?
faqs.answer: Doctors seeing Romanian patients hold registration with the Colegiul Medicilor din România, stated on each doctor's profile.

faqs.question: Is the certificate valid for medical leave?
faqs.answer: It records the medical assessment carried out. Medical leave and allowance are decided by CNAS and your employer against their own requirements.

faqs.question: What should I do in an emergency?
faqs.answer: Global Health is not an emergency service. Call 112 or attend the nearest emergency unit.

title: Dr Alexandra Paga - Pediatrician | Global Health
description: Dr. Alexandra Palaga, pediatric specialist physician, expert in gastroenterology and celiac disease. Online consultations for children.
h2: Need to schedule with this doctor?
What patients say about our doctors

faqs.question: Is Dr. Palaga registered with the Romanian College of Physicians?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dr. Alexandra Palaga is registered with the Romanian College of Physicians (CMR) under number 159625. You can verify this registration on the website cmr.ro. Dr. Palaga is a pediatric specialist certified by the Ministry of Health of Romania, a graduate of UMF Carol Davila, and a trainee member of ESPGHAN.

faqs.question: What pediatric conditions does Dr. Palaga evaluate online?
faqs.answer: Dr. Palaga offers online pediatric consultations for: general child health (from birth to 18 years), pediatric emergencies and evaluation of acute symptoms, pediatric gastroenterology (digestive issues, chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain), celiac disease (evaluation, investigations, dietary management), pediatric nutrition (selective eating, malnutrition, metabolic disorders), newborn and infant health, pediatric infectious diseases, growth and development assessment, and a second opinion on pediatric diagnoses or treatments.

faqs.question: Does Dr. Palaga have special expertise in celiac disease and pediatric gastroenterology?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dr. Palaga has worked as a research investigator at the Celiac Disease Management Center within the National Institute for Mother and Child Health "Alessandrescu-Rusescu" — the national reference center for this condition. Her work on nutritional strategies and gluten-free diets in children has been published in Frontiers in Pediatrics. She is a trainee member of ESPGHAN and has presented research at international ESPGHAN conferences. For families with children suspected of having celiac disease, food intolerance, or chronic digestive issues, this expertise is rarely available in an online consultation.

faqs.question: Can I book a pediatric consultation without a referral from my family doctor?
faqs.answer: Yes. Through Global Health Romania, you can directly book a consultation with Dr. Palaga without a referral from your family doctor or current pediatrician. If you have previous medical letters, test results, or investigations for your child, please send them before the consultation — they are not mandatory for booking, but they help with a more accurate assessment.

faqs.question: How do I book a consultation with Dr. Palaga?
faqs.answer: Select an available slot on this page to book directly with Dr. Palaga. Payment is securely processed at the time of booking — the consultation is confirmed after payment is made. You will immediately receive a calendar invitation. Consultations are conducted via secure video call in Romanian or English. We ask parents to have the child present for the consultation where possible.

faqs.question: What are Dr. Palaga's qualifications and research experience?
faqs.answer: Dr. Alexandra Palaga is a graduate of UMF Carol Davila in Bucharest and completed her residency in Pediatrics at the "Sf. Ioan" Emergency Clinical Hospital for Children in Galați and at the "Sf. Ioan" Emergency Clinical Hospital in Bucharest. She has worked as a research investigator at INSMCA "Alessandrescu-Rusescu" and has published in Frontiers in Pediatrics. She is a trainee member of ESPGHAN and a speaker at international ESPGHAN congresses and the European Academy of Pediatrics Societies. She is registered with CMR (no. 159625).

title: Dr Andreea Lorena Bica - Neurologist | Global Health
description: Dr. Andreea-Lorena Bica, specialist neurologist with experience in stroke, epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases. Schedule an online consultation.
h2: Need to schedule with this doctor?
What patients say about our doctors

faqs.question: Is Dr. Bica registered with the Romanian College of Physicians?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dr. Andreea-Lorena Bica is registered with the Colegiul Medicilor din România (CMR) under number 147502. You can verify this registration on the website cmr.ro. Dr. Bica is a specialist in Neurology, trained at the Elias University Emergency Hospital in Bucharest, and has contributed as a co-author to presentations at the European Academy of Neurology (EAN) Congress.

faqs.question: What neurological conditions does Dr. Bica evaluate online?
faqs.answer: Dr. Bica offers online neurological consultations for: stroke and cerebrovascular diseases (secondary evaluation, prevention, interpretation of investigations), epilepsy (evaluation and treatment adjustment), neurodegenerative diseases (Parkinson's, dementia, multiple sclerosis), headaches and migraines, peripheral neuropathies (numbness, tingling, weakness), movement disorders, the neurology-psychiatry interface, second opinions on diagnoses or MRI/CT results, and interpretation of neurological investigations.

faqs.question: Do I need a referral from my family doctor to consult a neurologist online?
faqs.answer: No. Through Global Health Romania, you can directly book a consultation with Dr. Bica without a referral from your family doctor. If you have previous medical letters, MRI results, EEG, or other investigations, please send them before the consultation — these are not mandatory for booking, but they help in making a more accurate assessment.

faqs.question: Can Dr. Bica explain the results of a brain MRI or other neurological investigations?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dr. Bica has specialized training in neuroimaging and neuroradiology and can interpret and explain the results of brain and spinal MRIs, CTs, EEGs, and other neurological investigations as part of the online consultation. If you send the radiology report or medical letter before the appointment, Dr. Bica will be able to provide a more detailed assessment.

faqs.question: How do I book a consultation with Dr. Bica?
faqs.answer: Select an available slot on this page to book directly with Dr. Bica. Payment is securely processed at the time of booking — the consultation is confirmed after payment is made. You will immediately receive a calendar invitation. Consultations are conducted via secure video call in Romanian or English. Please send any medical letters, MRI results, or EEGs before the consultation for a more accurate assessment. If you experience a neurological emergency — sudden and severe headache, acute weakness, or speech disturbances — call 112 immediately.

faqs.question: What are Dr. Bica's qualifications?
faqs.answer: Dr. Andreea-Lorena Bica graduated from the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Medicine and Pharmacy in Craiova and completed her residency in Neurology at the Elias University Emergency Hospital in Bucharest. She has participated as a co-author in research presentations at the Congress of the Romanian Society of Neurology and at the European Academy of Neurology (EAN) Congress. She is registered with the Colegiul Medicilor din România (CMR nr. 147502).

Dr. Brînduș works as a family doctor on the Global Health Romania platform, bringing specialized training in Anesthesia and Intensive Care — with experience at the Floreasca Emergency Clinical Hospital in Bucharest, Tallaght University Hospital, and Mater Misericordiae Dublin.What does Dr. Brînduș treat?Dr. Brînduș offers family medicine consultations covering acute conditions (respiratory infections, fever, flu, sore throat, urinary infections), management of chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes, asthma, reflux, cholesterol, hypothyroidism), dermatological issues, men's and women's health, mental health (anxiety, depression, stress), preventive care, pain management, preoperative advice, prescription renewals, medical certificates, and referrals.What does the ICU training bring to an online family doctor?Training in Anesthesia and Intensive Care means that Dr. Brînduș has managed some of the most complex and urgent medical situations — in operating rooms, intensive care units, and emergencies. This provides him with the ability to quickly assess the severity of a symptom, identify warning signs, and know precisely when a situation can be managed online and when it requires immediate emergency care. For a doctor consulting online, this clinical clarity is extremely valuable.Can Dr. Brînduș provide advice regarding a planned surgery or postoperative recovery?Yes. His training in ICU and perioperative medicine allows him to answer questions related to preoperative preparation, explain aspects related to anesthesia, assess risks, and provide guidance regarding postoperative recovery. If you have a scheduled procedure and would like a preliminary consultation or a second opinion, Dr. Brînduș can provide an informed assessment.How do I book a consultation with Dr. Brînduș?Select an available slot on this page to book directly with Dr. Brînduș. Payment is securely processed at the time of booking — the consultation is confirmed after payment is made. You will immediately receive a calendar invitation. Consultations take place via secure video call in Romanian, English, or Spanish. Same-day appointments are usually available.What are Dr. Brînduș's qualifications?Dr. Robert Brînduș is a graduate of the Faculty of Medicine at UMF Craiova. He completed his residency in ICU at the Floreasca Emergency Clinical Hospital in Bucharest and continued his training as an ICU registrar at Tallaght University Hospital and Mater Misericordiae University Hospital in Dublin, Ireland. He holds the European Diploma in Anesthesia and Intensive Care (EDAIC), Part I. body: Global Health · RomaniaGlobal Health · RomaniaQuestions, answered without the marketing speak.Booking, payment, consultations, privacy, and when online care is not the right route. Can't find what you need? Drop us a line.Contact the teamBook a consultationRomaniaBookingConsultationsMedical leave & prescriptionsPrivacyPaymentsRomaniaAbout our service in Romania01Do you have a clinic in Romania?Global Health operates in Romania as an online-only clinic. We hold no physical premises in Romania, and the company's registered office is in Ireland. Every consultation takes place over a secure video call, from a phone, tablet or computer, so there is no waiting room to visit. This online model lets you speak with a doctor without traveling, often on the same day you book. If you would rather see a doctor in person, a local clinic may suit you better — our platform is built for patients comfortable with a remote, video-based consultation instead.02Are the doctors registered in Romania?Yes. Every doctor who consults patients from Romania through our platform is registered with the Colegiul Medicilor din România, the body that regulates the medical profession in the country. Each doctor's registration, specialty and consultation languages are shown on their profile, so you can check before booking. This means the doctor you speak with meets the same professional and ethical standards as a doctor seen in person at a Romanian clinic. If you have a question about a specific doctor's registration, you can email us before booking and our team will confirm the relevant details for you.03Are consultations available in Romanian?Yes. Consultations for patients in Romania are held in Romanian, and several doctors also consult in English. Each doctor's profile lists the languages they speak, so you can pick a doctor who matches your preference before booking. Administrative support — bookings, billing, account questions — is also handled by email in both Romanian and English. If a particular language matters for your consultation itself, check the doctor's profile before confirming your appointment, or write to us and we can point you toward a doctor who consults in the language you need.Still stuckNot the question you came with?
